lessons.title: Resultant force and acceleration
lessons.summary: Relate a signed force sum to acceleration and use that acceleration in straight-line motion.
lessons.objective: Relate a signed force sum to acceleration and use that acceleration in straight-line motion.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Forces and equilibrium
  • Kinematics
lessons.ideas:
Newton’s second law along the chosen axis is \(\sum F=ma\). The force on the left is the net force on the chosen mass. Use newtons for the forces, kilograms for the mass and metres per second squared for the acceleration.

With right as positive, a larger resistance than thrust makes the acceleration negative. The fact that the trolley is travelling right fixes the direction of the resistance at that instant.

For thrust \(P\) and a leftward resistance of magnitude \(R\), use \(P-R=ma\). The minus sign is part of the component equation. A computed negative magnitude would contradict the assumed direction.

For a fixed positive direction, \(v=u+at\) uses the signed acceleration and signed velocities. Check that the movement stays on the assumed branch if the resistance direction was chosen using the initial velocity.

In straight-line motion, constant velocity gives \(a=0\). When the only horizontal forces are drive and resistance, this gives \(P=R\). Vertical balance should be checked separately.
lessons.method:
Relate a signed force sum to acceleration and use that acceleration in straight-line motion.

  • Find the signed resultant
  • Separate velocity from acceleration
  • Write the force equation before solving
  • Pass the acceleration into kinematics
  • Check the zero-resultant case
mistakes: If a driving force and a resistance both act, the driving force on its own is not the resultant.
Do not turn a resistance arrow round simply because the acceleration is negative.
Substituting a negative acceleration into the equation does not mean changing the sign written for each force.
The motion equations contain velocity and time, not the driving force.
Motion alone does not imply there is a nonzero resultant.

examples.title: Find a positive resultant
examples.question: A \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(43\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(11\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
examples.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=43-11=32\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=4\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Find negative acceleration during forward motion
examples.question: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. Its driving force is \(18\, \mathrm N\) and its resistance is \(36\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed resultant and acceleration.
examples.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=18-36=-18\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=-\frac{3}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

examples.title: Recover an unknown resistance
examples.question: A \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. The thrust is \(38\, \mathrm N\) and the constant acceleration is \(\frac{5}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the resistance.
examples.solution:
\(38-R=10\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)\). The resistance contributes a negative component.

Solving gives \(R=13\, \mathrm N\). The answer is a magnitude and acts left.

examples.title: Use force to predict a final velocity
examples.question: A \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) instrument trolley travels right on a level test track. Take right as positive. It initially moves at \(4\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). For \(3\, \mathrm s\) the thrust is \(40\, \mathrm N\) and resistance is \(22\, \mathrm N\). Find its signed acceleration and the final velocity.
examples.solution:
\(F_\mathrm{net}=40-22=18\) in newtons, because the thrust points right and the resistance points left.

\(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) by dividing the signed resultant by the trolley mass.

\(v=u+at=4+\left(2\right)(3)\) gives \(v=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

lessons.title: Vertical motion and lift forces
lessons.summary: Use signed vertical acceleration to find and interpret a normal reaction.
lessons.objective: Use signed vertical acceleration to find and interpret a normal reaction.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Resultant force and acceleration
lessons.ideas:
With upwards positive, \(R-mg=ma\). The weight is \(mg\) and does not change just because the lift accelerates. The reaction changes to provide the net force required.

If a lift is moving down and slowing, its acceleration is upwards. Use the stated acceleration or infer its sign from the change in velocity, then compare \(R\) with \(mg\).

Rearrange \(R-mg=ma\) to get \(a=\frac Rm-g\). Compare the sign with the size of the reading and give the direction if asked.

At \(R=0\) the parcel has \(a=-g\) relative to an upward positive axis. If the lift floor accelerates down faster than free fall, the parcel loses contact and the two accelerations differ.

Write a new equation for each constant-acceleration stage. The weight is constant across stages. The reaction can be greater than, equal to or less than the weight.
lessons.method:
Use signed vertical acceleration to find and interpret a normal reaction.

  • Select the body
  • Interpret the sign of acceleration
  • Work backwards from apparent weight
  • Check the contact condition
  • Separate steady and accelerating stages
mistakes: Do not include the cable tension when resolving forces acting on the parcel alone.
A lift moving downwards does not necessarily have downward acceleration.
A force reading is measured in newtons. It is not the mass of the object.
Do not report a negative normal reaction as though it were a downward force exerted by the floor.
A lift travelling steadily upwards does not require an upward resultant.

examples.title: Find the floor reaction while accelerating upwards
examples.question: A \(12\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
examples.solution:
\(W=120\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=144\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

examples.title: Compare reaction to weight during downward acceleration
examples.question: A \(15\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(-3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
examples.solution:
\(W=150\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=-3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=105\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

examples.title: Determine acceleration from a scale reading
examples.question: A \(20\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The floor exerts an upward normal force of \(230\, \mathrm N\). Find the signed acceleration.
examples.solution:
\(W=200\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=\frac{3}{2}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=230\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

examples.title: Find the reaction in free fall
examples.question: A \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) parcel remains in contact with the floor of a lift. Take upwards as positive and use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The signed acceleration is \(-10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the weight of the parcel and the normal force from the floor.
examples.solution:
\(W=90\, \mathrm N\) acts downwards and the reaction acts upwards.

\(R-mg=ma\). Keep the signs in this relation even if the lift is moving downwards.

\(a=-10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(R=0\, \mathrm N\) satisfy the vertical equation.

lessons.title: Dynamics on a rough inclined plane
lessons.summary: Use perpendicular balance and direction-dependent friction to determine along-plane acceleration.
lessons.objective: Use perpendicular balance and direction-dependent friction to determine along-plane acceleration.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Forces and equilibrium
  • Resultant force and acceleration
lessons.ideas:
For a slope at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, weight contributes \(mg\sin\theta\) down the plane and \(mg\cos\theta\) into it. Use the angle from the slope to determine which component is adjacent and which is opposite.

While the particle slides, the model uses magnitude \(\mu R\). Keep the same axis uphill when comparing the two directions. The component of weight along the plane keeps its negative sign.

For an uphill pull of magnitude \(P\) and uphill movement, \(P-mg\sin\theta-\mu R=ma\). If the particle moves downhill, friction enters with a plus sign instead.

Write \(R+F_\perp-mg\cos\theta=0\) for an outward component. Check \(R\ge0\). Substitute the resulting reaction into the uphill force equation.

At each sliding stage, apply the force equation to identify its own constant acceleration. Use the appropriate motion formulae only within that stage.
lessons.method:
Use perpendicular balance and direction-dependent friction to determine along-plane acceleration.

  • Resolve parallel and perpendicular to the plane
  • Choose friction using velocity
  • Add all signed along-plane forces
  • Recalculate the reaction
  • Rebuild the force equation after a reversal
mistakes: The normal reaction equals the perpendicular component of weight only when no other force contributes to that axis.
A box can slide down the plane while its acceleration points up. That motion is slowing.
Do not add a pull to the reaction if it acts exactly parallel to the plane.
Using the old value of the normal force gives the wrong friction after the pull changes.
Do not use the uphill equation through the instant of reversal and on down the plane.

examples.title: Resolve a weight on a slope
examples.question: A \(5\, \mathrm{kg}\) box moves up a rough plane at an instant. The plane makes angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\). Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take up the plane as positive. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the normal reaction and the signed acceleration.
examples.solution:
Perpendicular to the surface there is no acceleration. Hence \(R=mg\cos\theta\) gives \(40\, \mathrm N\).

The sliding friction has magnitude \(\mu R\) = \(10\, \mathrm N\) and acts down the plane.

\(ma=0-30-10\) after resolving along the plane.

\(a=-8\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) with the stated positive direction.

examples.title: Reverse the friction direction on descent
examples.question: A \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\) box moves down a rough plane at an instant. The plane makes angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\). Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take up the plane as positive. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{5}\). Find the normal reaction and the signed acceleration.
examples.solution:
Perpendicular to the surface there is no acceleration. Hence \(R=mg\cos\theta\) gives \(80\, \mathrm N\).

The sliding friction has magnitude \(\mu R\) = \(16\, \mathrm N\) and acts up the plane.

\(ma=0-60+16\) after resolving along the plane.

\(a=-\frac{22}{5}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) with the stated positive direction.

examples.title: Include an uphill pull
examples.question: A \(13\, \mathrm{kg}\) box moves up a rough plane at an instant. The plane makes angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal, where \(\sin\theta=\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac{12}{13}\). Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take up the plane as positive. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). There is also a force of \(110\, \mathrm N\) parallel to and up the plane. Find the normal reaction and the signed acceleration.
examples.solution:
Perpendicular to the surface there is no acceleration. Hence \(R=mg\cos\theta\) gives \(120\, \mathrm N\).

The sliding friction has magnitude \(\mu R\) = \(30\, \mathrm N\) and acts down the plane.

\(ma=110-50-30\) after resolving along the plane.

\(a=\frac{30}{13}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) with the stated positive direction.

examples.title: A pull lifts partly away from the slope
examples.question: A \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) slider is travelling up a rough slope. The angle satisfies \(\sin\theta=\frac35\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac45\). A pull has an up-slope component \(74\, \mathrm N\) and a component \(16\, \mathrm N\) acting perpendicularly away from the surface. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and coefficient of friction \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the reaction and the signed acceleration with uphill positive.
examples.solution:
\(R+F_\perp=mg\cos\theta\) perpendicular to the surface, so \(R=48\, \mathrm N\).

The direction of motion is uphill. Friction therefore has downhill magnitude \(F=12\, \mathrm N\).

\(ma=F_\parallel-mg\sin\theta-\mu R\) gives \(a=\frac{7}{4}\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

lessons.title: Connected particles in a straight line
lessons.summary: Find the common acceleration and distinguish pull, push and slack connection models.
lessons.objective: Find the common acceleration and distinguish pull, push and slack connection models.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Resultant force and acceleration
lessons.ideas:
For the combined system the connector pulls or pushes between its parts. Those forces cancel internally. Divide the sum of the external force components by the total mass to find the common acceleration.

If the connector pulls the rear vehicle to the right, write \(T-R_2=m_2a\). Substitute the common signed acceleration. Use the front vehicle to check that the same magnitude acts the opposite way.

Positive connector force on the rear means tension in this orientation. Negative means compression, with magnitude given by the absolute value. A rope under a negative result would go slack instead.

Calculate the signed external force divided by mass for each vehicle. If these values already agree, the connected model gives zero connector force.

Solve for \(T\) using the stated positive direction. When \(T>0\) the rope assumption is consistent. If it becomes slack in a later stage, give each vehicle its own force equation.
lessons.method:
Find the common acceleration and distinguish pull, push and slack connection models.

  • Start with the whole system
  • Isolate one vehicle
  • Interpret the sign of the connector force
  • Compare the independent accelerations
  • Check tension and net force separately
mistakes: Using the mass of only the lead vehicle with the external forces from both vehicles gives the wrong acceleration.
Using the whole pair to find tension makes the unknown disappear from the equation.
Do not describe a negative magnitude as a negative tension.
A decreasing speed does not automatically imply compression. The distribution of drive and resistance matters.
A negative common acceleration does not imply a negative rope force.

examples.title: Find common acceleration and rope tension
examples.question: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light taut inextensible rope. The leading vehicle has mass \(14\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(55\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(13\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(8\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(9\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
examples.solution:
\(a=\frac{55-13-9}{22}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-9=8\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(21\, \mathrm N\). Tension therefore has magnitude \(21\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

examples.title: A different acceleration still produces a pull
examples.question: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light taut inextensible rope. The leading vehicle has mass \(11\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(49\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(16\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(7\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
examples.solution:
\(a=\frac{49-16-7}{17}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-7=6\left(\frac{26}{17}\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(\frac{275}{17}\, \mathrm N\). Tension therefore has magnitude \(\frac{275}{17}\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

examples.title: Slow with a rigid bar in compression
examples.question: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light rigid tow-bar. The leading vehicle has mass \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(0\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(40\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(4\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
examples.solution:
\(a=\frac{0-40-4}{16}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-4=6\left(-\frac{11}{4}\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(-\frac{25}{2}\, \mathrm N\). Compression therefore has magnitude \(\frac{25}{2}\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

examples.title: A moving rigid connection can exert no force
examples.question: Two vehicles move to the right on a horizontal line, joined by a light rigid tow-bar. The leading vehicle has mass \(10\, \mathrm{kg}\), thrust \(5\, \mathrm N\) and resistance \(15\, \mathrm N\). The rear vehicle has mass \(5\, \mathrm{kg}\) and resistance \(5\, \mathrm N\). Take right as positive. Find their common acceleration and the magnitude of the connection force. State whether the connection is in tension or compression, or exerts zero force.
examples.solution:
\(a=\frac{5-15-5}{15}\) for the whole system. The connector forces are internal to this system.

On the rear vehicle, the signed horizontal force from the connector satisfies \(T-5=5\left(-1\right)\).

The signed connector force on the rear vehicle is \(0\, \mathrm N\). Zero connection force therefore has magnitude \(0\, \mathrm N\).

The force on the front vehicle from the connector has the same magnitude and the opposite direction in this ideal light model.

lessons.title: Pulley models and changes of constraint
lessons.summary: Solve a linked pulley model, then find the new motion if the string becomes slack.
lessons.objective: Solve a linked pulley model, then find the new motion if the string becomes slack.
lessons.before:
Check that you can substitute into a function and read a graph with signed coordinates.

  • Connected particles in a straight line
  • Kinematics
lessons.ideas:
For two hanging bodies, choose a positive axis downwards for the heavier one and upwards for the lighter one. This puts the same positive acceleration magnitude in both equations when the assumed motion occurs.

\(m_2g-T=m_2a\) and \(T-m_1g=m_1a\). Adding removes the internal pull. Substitute the resulting acceleration into either equation and check the other equation.

Choose the box’s positive direction towards the pulley and the hanging mass’s positive direction downwards. Take resistance away from the pulley when the box moves towards it.

When the table resistance exceeds the driving weight under the assumed configuration, the acceleration sign changes. Decide how friction is directed using the stated motion. If a particle starts at rest, the question may require a static-friction check first.

Find the boundary speed under the first acceleration. Use that speed as the initial speed of the continuing body. Redraw the forces and find its new acceleration. Use the constant-acceleration equations only within each stage.
lessons.method:
Solve a linked pulley model, then find the new motion if the string becomes slack.

  • Choose a positive direction for each body
  • Eliminate tension and substitute back
  • Keep the table resistance and hanger weight separate
  • Check force directions and magnitudes
  • Split the motion into constrained and free stages
mistakes: Using one global vertical sign in both equations requires opposite signed accelerations. Do not combine a global axis with equal signed accelerations.
Using the weight difference with only one mass gives the wrong acceleration.
The weight of the block on a horizontal table does not appear directly as a horizontal resistance.
A negative computed acceleration does not justify turning all arrows around without examining the physical question.
Do not reuse the combined mass or tension in the second equation when the string is slack.

examples.title: Use matching acceleration magnitudes
examples.question: Masses \(3\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(7\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(7\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
examples.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(70-T=7a\). The first is \(T-30=3a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(40=10a\), hence \(a=4\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=42\, \mathrm N\).

examples.title: Find the tension after removing it from the combined equation
examples.question: Masses \(4\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(6\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
examples.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(60-T=6a\). The first is \(T-40=4a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(20=10a\), hence \(a=2\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=48\, \mathrm N\).

examples.title: Let the hanging mass pull a box along a rough table
examples.question: A \(9\, \mathrm{kg}\) box is on a horizontal table. A light inextensible string runs horizontally from it over a smooth pulley to a hanging \(6\, \mathrm{kg}\) mass. The resistance to sliding of the box is \(15\, \mathrm N\). The string is taut and the box moves towards the pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(6\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
examples.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and towards the pulley for the box.

The second equation is \(60-T=6a\). The first is \(T-15=9a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(45=15a\), hence \(a=3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=42\, \mathrm N\).

examples.title: Calculate the force on a second two-mass system
examples.question: Masses \(7\, \mathrm{kg}\) and \(13\, \mathrm{kg}\) hang on the two ends of a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley. Use \(g=10\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and take downwards for the hanging \(13\) kg mass. Give the common acceleration magnitude and tension.
examples.solution:
Use a separate positive axis for each object. Take downwards for the second mass and upwards for the lighter mass.

The second equation is \(130-T=13a\). The first is \(T-70=7a\).

Adding cancels the tension. It gives \(60=20a\), hence \(a=3\, \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Substitute that acceleration into one particle's equation. This gives \(T=91\, \mathrm N\).

For \(3\, \mathrm s\) the thrust is \(71\, \mathrm N\) and resistance is \(21\, \mathrm N\). Find its signed acceleration and the final velocity.
questions.solution_html:
